Cookbook

Source: vignettes/cookbook.Rmd
cookbook.Rmd

This vignette provides recipes for common tasks involving age group, period, and cohort labels. Each recipe describes a problem and gives a solution. For an overview of the agetime package, see Get started.

library(agetime)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(0)

Create and modify labels

Create labels from scratch

Problem

You need a new set of age group, period, or cohort labels.

Solution

For labels with regular widths, use functions such as age_labels_ten() or period_labels_five().

age_labels_ten()
#>  [1] "0-9"   "10-19" "20-29" "30-39" "40-49" "50-59" "60-69" "70-79" "80-89"
#> [10] "90-99" "100+"
period_labels_five(
  lower_first = 2001,
  lower_last = 2031
)
#> [1] "2001-2006" "2006-2011" "2011-2016" "2016-2021" "2021-2026" "2026-2031"
#> [7] "2031-2036"

For labels with irregular widths, use age_labels(), period_labels(), or cohort_labels(), and specify the breaks.

age_labels(
  breaks = c(0, 20, 65, 100)
)
#> [1] "0-19"  "20-64" "65-99" "100+"
cohort_labels(
  breaks = c(2000, 2010, 2030),
  open_left = TRUE
)
#> [1] "<2000"     "2000-2010" "2010-2030"

Discussion

There is no universally accepted set of conventions on how age, period, and cohort labels should be formatted. agetime tries to reflect common practices in demography and official statistics.

See Also

  • The help pages for age_labels(), period_labels(), and cohort_labels() describe agetime formatting rules

Standardize labels

Problem

Your age, period, or cohort labels come in a mix of formats, such as "5to9", "10--14", and "100plus", and you want them all in one consistent format.

Solution

Use age_standard(), period_standard(), or cohort_standard().

df <- tibble(
  age = c("5to9", "10--14", "100plus", "infants"),
  count = c(11, 9, 2, 22)
)

df |>
  mutate(age = age_standard(age))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   age   count
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 5-9      11
#> 2 10-14     9
#> 3 100+      2
#> 4 0        22

The standard functions recognize the formats commonly found in published tables, including totals and not-stated categories.

age_standard(c("All ages", "Under 1", "1-4 years", "Age 5 to 9",
               "10-14yrs", "85 years and over", "Not stated"))
#> [1] "Total" "0"     "1-4"   "5-9"   "10-14" "85+"   NA

Discussion

If the labels argument is a factor, then the standard functions standardize the factor levels along with the values.

Not-stated categories become NA. To remove them, see Drop “Not stated” categories from a dataset.

See Also

  • The help pages for age_standard(), period_standard(), and cohort_standard() describe agetime formatting rules

Convert lower limits to age group labels

Problem

Your data store age groups as numbers, such as 0, 5, 10, …, 85, where each number is the lower limit of a five-year age group, and 85 is the lower limit of an open age group. You want age group labels such as "0-4" and "85+".

Solution

Treat the numbers as single years, coarsen them to five-year groups, and then make the last group open.

age <- c(0, 5, 10, 80, 85)
age |>
  age_coarsen_five() |>
  age_set_open_right(at = 85)
#> [1] 0-4   5-9   10-14 80-84 85+  
#> Levels: 0-4 5-9 10-14 80-84 85+

For life-table age groups, where the numbers are 0, 1, 5, 10, …, use age_coarsen_life() in place of age_coarsen_five().

Discussion

agetime reads a number on its own as a single year of age. Without coarsening, 5 is the interval from age 5 up to age 6, not up to age 10.

age_interval(age)
#> [1] "[0, 1)"   "[5, 6)"   "[10, 11)" "[80, 81)" "[85, 86)"

See Also

  • Aggregate to broader age groups
  • Specify an open-ended age group, period, or cohort

Adopt coarser age groups from another age variable

Problem

You have two age variables, and you want to switch the finer one to the coarser age groups used by the other.

Solution

Use age_coarsen_to().

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0", "1", "5", "10", "11"),
  n = c(3, 1, 4, 6, 7)
)
age_wide <- c("0-4", "5-14")

df |>
  mutate(age = age_coarsen_to(age, to = age_wide)) |>
  count(age, wt = n)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <fct> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4       4
#> 2 5-14     17

Discussion

Every age group in labels must lie inside exactly one age group in to. Otherwise age_coarsen_to() throws an error, which distinguishes two problems:

  • an age group would be split when it overlaps two or more age groups in to, as "5-9" overlaps "0-6" and "7-14";
  • an age group is not fully covered when part of it lies outside all the age groups in to, as "20" lies above "7-14".
age_coarsen_to(c("0-4", "5-9", "20"), to = c("0-6", "7-14"))
#> Error in `age_coarsen_to()`:
#> ! Can't coarsen age groups.
#> ✖ Age group "5-9" would be split by the labels in `to`.
#> ℹ "5-9" overlaps "0-6" and "7-14".
#> ✖ Age group "20" is not fully covered by the labels in `to`.
#> ℹ Add labels to `to` that cover it?

See Also

  • Aggregate to broader age groups
  • Build a mapping between age groups
  • period_coarsen_to(), cohort_coarsen_to()

Create labels for a forecast

Problem

You have labels for past periods, and you need labels for future periods, for use in a forecast.

Solution

Use period_extend().

recent <- c("2020-2025", "2025-2030")
period_extend(recent, n = 2)
#> [1] "2020-2025" "2025-2030" "2030-2035" "2035-2040"

See Also

  • age_extend() extends age groups and cohort_extend() extends cohorts.

Specify an open-ended age group, period, or cohort

Problem

You want an open interval at one end of your labels, with a limit specified by you. The labels might already have an open interval with a different limit, or they might not have one at all.

An open interval is one that has no lower limit (e.g. "<2000") or no upper limit (e.g. "85+").

Solution

Use

  • age_set_open_right(),
  • period_set_open_left(),
  • period_set_open_right(),
  • cohort_set_open_left(), or
  • cohort_set_open_right().
labels_age <- c("0-4", "60-64", "90+")
age_set_open_right(labels_age, at = 80)
#> [1] 0-4   60-64 80+  
#> Levels: 0-4 60-64 80+

Discussion

The set_open functions always return factors. If you would prefer a character vector, call as.character() on the result,

labels_age |>
  age_set_open_right(at = 80) |>
  as.character()
#> [1] "0-4"   "60-64" "80+"

See Also

  • Use
    • age_is_open_right(),
    • period_is_open_left(),
    • period_is_open_right(),
    • cohort_is_open_left(), or
    • cohort_is_open_right()
    to identify open intervals.
  • The coarsen, fill, and set_order functions, like the set_open functions, always return factors

Create an age variable that sorts properly

Problem

Raw age group labels sort in alphabetical order:

df <- tibble(
  age = c("10-14", "0-4", "5-9"),
  count = c(33, 7, 15)
)

df |>
  arrange(age) ## "10-14" comes before "5-9"!!
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age   count
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4       7
#> 2 10-14    33
#> 3 5-9      15

You want an age variable that sorts in age order.

Solution

Function age_set_order() creates a factor with levels in the right order.

labels_unordered <- c("10-14", "0-4", "5-9")
age_set_order(labels_unordered)
#> [1] 10-14 0-4   5-9  
#> Levels: 0-4 5-9 10-14

Discussion

If labels is not a factor, age_set_order() turns it into one.

See Also

  • Use period_set_order() and cohort_set_order() to make period and cohort labels sort in the right order.
  • Order by age when working interactively
  • The set_open, coarsen, and fill functions, like the set_order functions, always return factors

Ensure that all age groups appear in a table

Problem

You are building a table, and you want it to show every age group, including age groups with no observations.

Solution

Generate the full set of labels with

  • age_labels(),
  • age_labels_one(),
  • age_labels_five(),
  • age_labels_ten(), or
  • age_labels_life(),

then join the data on to the set.

all_ages <- tibble(
  age = age_labels_five(
    lower_first = 0,
    lower_last = 20,
    open_right = FALSE
  )
)

observed <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "10-14"),
  n = c(30, 25)
)

all_ages |>
  left_join(observed, by = "age")
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4      30
#> 2 5-9      NA
#> 3 10-14    25
#> 4 15-19    NA
#> 5 20-24    NA

Alternatively, to fill gaps between the age groups in the data, use a fill function, then complete() from the tidyr package.

library(tidyr)

observed |>
  mutate(age = age_fill_five(age)) |>
  complete(age, fill = list(n = 0))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <fct> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4      30
#> 2 5-9       0
#> 3 10-14    25

complete() sorts character vectors alphabetically, so age needs to be a factor, as it is here.

Discussion

age_labels_life() creates the labels used by an abridged life table, "0", "1-4", "5-9", "10-14", …

See Also

  • Periods and cohorts have equivalent labels functions.
  • The fill functions (e.g. age_fill_five()) add intermediate levels to a factor.
  • Create an age variable that sorts properly
  • Include levels that don’t appear in the data

Check labels

Check for gaps, overlaps, and other problems

Problem

You want to check that a set of labels meets your expectations, such as having no gaps, and either report any problems or stop a pipeline.

Solution

Use the diagnose_values functions for diagnostics. Use the assert_values functions to throw an error as soon as a condition is violated.

lab <- c("2020-2025", "2025-2030", "2030-2035")
period_diagnose_values(lab, no_gap = TRUE, no_overlap = TRUE)
#> $ok
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $details
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   condition  passed comment
#>   <chr>      <lgl>  <chr>  
#> 1 no_overlap TRUE   NA     
#> 2 no_gap     TRUE   NA

pop <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "5-9", "10-14"),
  count = c(100, 110, 105)
)

pop |>
  mutate(age = age_assert_values(age, has_zero = TRUE, no_gap = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age   count
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4     100
#> 2 5-9     110
#> 3 10-14   105

Discussion

The diagnose functions return a list with an ok flag and details.

The assert functions return their input invisibly when checks pass. Returning their inputs allows them to be used in pipelines.

The values functions treat each element of labels as a separate group, so a label that appears more than once counts as overlapping.

See Also

  • ?age_diagnose_levels, ?period_diagnose_levels, or ?cohort_diagnose_levels for the full set of conditions
  • Check labels within groups of a data frame
  • Check the levels of a factor

Check labels within groups of a data frame

Problem

Your data frame has one row for each combination of age group and another variable, such as sex, and you want to check the age groups for each sex. Checking the whole column fails, because each age group appears more than once.

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "5-9", "0-4", "5-9"),
  sex = c("F", "F", "M", "M"),
  count = c(51, 49, 53, 50)
)

df |>
  mutate(age = age_assert_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE))
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `age = age_assert_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE)`.
#> Caused by error in `age_assert_values()`:
#> ! Age group labels fail check `no_overlap`.
#> ✖ `no_overlap`: Example of overlap among values: '0-4' appears 2 times. To
#>   allow repeats, such as one per sex, check within groups, for instance using
#>   dplyr::group_by().

Solution

Group the data first, for instance using group_by().

df |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  mutate(age = age_assert_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE, has_zero = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#> # Groups:   sex [2]
#>   age   sex   count
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4   F        51
#> 2 5-9   F        49
#> 3 0-4   M        53
#> 4 5-9   M        50

Discussion

Every check is applied separately to each group. For instance, has_zero = TRUE checks that each sex has an age group starting at zero.

See Also

  • Check for gaps, overlaps, and other problems

Check the levels of a factor

Problem

Your labels are a factor, and you want to check the levels, including levels that do not appear in the data.

Solution

Use the diagnose_levels and assert_levels functions.

age <- factor(
  c("0-4", "0-4", "5-9"),
  levels = c("0-4", "5-9", "10+")
)

age_diagnose_levels(age, no_overlap = TRUE, has_open_right = TRUE)
#> $ok
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $details
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   condition      passed comment
#>   <chr>          <lgl>  <chr>  
#> 1 no_overlap     TRUE   NA     
#> 2 has_open_right TRUE   NA
age_diagnose_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE, has_open_right = TRUE)
#> $ok
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $details
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   condition      passed comment                                                 
#>   <chr>          <lgl>  <chr>                                                   
#> 1 no_overlap     FALSE  Example of overlap among values: '0-4' appears 2 times.…
#> 2 has_open_right FALSE  Highest interval among values: '5-9'

Discussion

The levels functions throw an error if labels is not a factor.

See Also

  • Include levels that don’t appear in the data

See the intervals implied by a set of labels

Problem

You are not sure how agetime is interpreting a set of labels. For instance, does "2020" refer to the year starting in 2020 or the year ending in 2020, and does "2020-2024" include 2024?

Solution

Use the interval functions, which describe each label using interval notation.

age_interval(c("0", "1-4", "5-9", "100+"))
#> [1] "[0, 1)"     "[1, 5)"     "[5, 10)"    "[100, Inf)"

period_interval(c("2018", "2019", "2020-2025"))
#> [1] "[2018, 2019)" "[2019, 2020)" "[2020, 2025)"

To see how the interpretation changes, vary interpret_single and interpret_multi.

## years running from 1 July to 30 June, with
## labels giving the year in which they end
period_interval(c("2019", "2020"), interpret_single = "upper")
#> [1] "[2018, 2019)" "[2019, 2020)"

## second number in "2020-2024" is the last year
## in the interval, rather than the upper limit
cohort_interval(c("2015-2019", "2020-2024"), interpret_multi = "below_upper")
#> [1] "[2015, 2020)" "[2020, 2025)"

Discussion

In interval notation, a square bracket means that the interval includes the limit, and a round bracket means that the interval excludes it. Age "5-9", for instance, is "[5, 10)", which includes people who have reached their 5th birthday but not their 10th. The limit of an open interval is written -Inf or Inf, as in "[100, Inf)".

The interval functions return descriptions of labels, not labels, and other agetime functions cannot read them.

See Also

  • ?age_interval, ?period_interval, and ?cohort_interval
  • The lower, upper, width, and mid functions (e.g. period_lower()) return the limits, widths, and midpoints of intervals as numbers
  • Check for gaps, overlaps, and other problems

Analyse data

Filter rows by age, period, or cohort

Problem

You want to keep rows from your dataset for certain ages, periods, or cohorts, and discard the rest. But the age, period, and cohort labels are strings, so you can’t compare them with numbers.

Solution

Filter on lower or upper limits.

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-14", "15-64", "65+", "Total"),
  period = c("2017", "2033", "2050+", "2020-2030"),
  count = c(100, 200, 50, 350)
)

df |>
  filter(age_lower(age) >= 15)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   age   period count
#>   <chr> <chr>  <dbl>
#> 1 15-64 2033     200
#> 2 65+   2050+     50

df |>
  filter(period_upper(period) <= 2030)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   age   period    count
#>   <chr> <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 0-14  2017        100
#> 2 Total 2020-2030   350

See Also

  • Use
    • age_is_total(),
    • period_is_total(), or
    • cohort_is_total()
    to filter out totals, and use
    • age_is_missing(),
    • period_is_missing(), or
    • cohort_is_missing()
    to filter out not-stated or missing values.

Drop totals from a dataset

Problem

Your dataset includes rows for totals, such as "All ages", which you want to remove.

Solution

Use age_is_total(), period_is_total(), or cohort_is_total() to identify rows with totals, and then filter.

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-14", "15-64", "65+", "All"),
  count = c(10, 20, 5, 35)
)

df |>
  filter(!age_is_total(age))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age   count
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 0-14     10
#> 2 15-64    20
#> 3 65+       5

Discussion

age_is_total(), period_is_total(), and cohort_is_total() recognize synonyms for totals (e.g. "all") and ignore case (e.g. "tOTaL").

See Also

  • Drop “Not stated” categories from a dataset

Drop “Not stated” categories from a dataset

Problem

Your dataset includes rows where age, period, or cohort is not stated or missing, and you want to remove them.

Solution

Use age_is_missing(), period_is_missing(), or cohort_is_missing() to identify rows with not stated or missing and then filter.

df <- tibble(
  time = c("2005", "unknown", "2005-2010", NA),
  count = c(100, 2, 55, 12)
)

df |>
  filter(!period_is_missing(time))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   time      count
#>   <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 2005        100
#> 2 2005-2010    55

Discussion

age_is_missing(), period_is_missing(), and cohort_is_missing() look for NAs, but also for text equivalents, such as "Not stated", "Don't know" or "n/a".

See Also

  • Drop totals from a dataset

Order by age when working interactively

Problem

You are exploring a dataset interactively, and you want to sort on age, but the age labels are sorted in alphabetical order.

df <- tibble(
  age_group = c("5-9", "0-4", "10-14"),
  count = c(33, 7, 15)
)

df |>
  arrange(age_group) ## "10-14" comes before "5-9"
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age_group count
#>   <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 0-4           7
#> 2 10-14        15
#> 3 5-9          33

Solution

Sort on lower or upper limits.

df <- tibble(
  age_group = c("5-9", "0-4", "10-14"),
  count = c(33, 7, 15)
)

df |>
  arrange(age_lower(age_group))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age_group count
#>   <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 0-4           7
#> 2 5-9          33
#> 3 10-14        15

Discussion

If you want the variable itself to sort in age order, use age_set_order(), period_set_order(), or cohort_set_order(). See Create an age variable that sorts properly.

Include levels that don’t appear in the data

Problem

Some age groups, periods, or cohorts don’t appear in your data, but you want them to appear in tabulations.

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "10-14", "0-4"),
  respondents = c(10, 20, 5)
)

## misses "5-9"
df |>
  count(age, wt = respondents)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4      15
#> 2 10-14    20

Solution

Use one of the fill functions such as age_fill_five().

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "10-14", "0-4"),
  respondents = c(10, 20, 5)
)

## includes 5-9
df |>
  mutate(age = age_fill_five(age)) |>
  count(age, wt = respondents, .drop = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <fct> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4      15
#> 2 5-9       0
#> 3 10-14    20

Discussion

The fill functions change the levels of labels, not the values. If labels is not a factor, the fill functions turn it into one.

Tidyverse functions such as count() and summarise() drop unused levels by default. If .drop = FALSE is not included in the call to count(), then the extra level added by age_fill_five() does not appear in the results,

df |>
  mutate(age = age_fill_five(age)) |>
  count(age, wt = respondents)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <fct> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4      15
#> 2 10-14    20

See Also

  • The full set of fill functions:
age_fill() period_fill() cohort_fill()
age_fill_one() period_fill_one() cohort_fill_one()
age_fill_five() period_fill_five() cohort_fill_five()
age_fill_ten() period_fill_ten() cohort_fill_ten()
age_fill_life()
  • age_set_order(), period_set_order(), cohort_set_order() put levels in the right order.

Aggregate to broader age groups

Problem

Your data use one-year age groups, and you want to aggregate to five-year age groups.

Solution

Convert to coarser labels, then aggregate.

deaths <- tibble(
  age = c("0", "1", "2", "5", "6", "10", "11"),
  n = c(3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7)
)
deaths
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 0         3
#> 2 1         1
#> 3 2         2
#> 4 5         4
#> 5 6         5
#> 6 10        6
#> 7 11        7

deaths |>
  mutate(age = age_coarsen_five(age)) |>
  count(age, wt = n)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <fct> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4       6
#> 2 5-9       9
#> 3 10-14    13

Discussion

For irregular age groups, use age_coarsen(). To borrow categories from another set of labels, use age_coarsen_to(). To aggregate to (abridged) life-table ages, use age_coarsen_life().

See Also

  • Adopt coarser age groups from another age variable
  • period_coarsen_five(), cohort_coarsen_five()
  • period_coarsen(), cohort_coarsen()
  • age_coarsen_to(), period_coarsen_to(), cohort_coarsen_to()

Build a mapping between age groups

Problem

You have two age classifications, and you want a lookup table showing how the age groups in one classification relate to the age groups in the other.

Solution

Use age_mapping().

classif_fine <- age_labels_ten(lower_last = 60)
classif_broad <- age_labels(breaks = c(0, 20, 60), open_right = TRUE)
age_mapping(
  labels_x = classif_fine,
  labels_y = classif_broad,
  relation = "is_contained_in"
)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>   x     y    
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 0-9   0-19 
#> 2 10-19 0-19 
#> 3 20-29 20-59
#> 4 30-39 20-59
#> 5 40-49 20-59
#> 6 50-59 20-59
#> 7 60+   60+

Discussion

Other possible values for relation are "equals", "contains", and "overlaps_with".

To represent the mapping as a matrix rather than a data frame, set format to "matrix",

age_mapping(
  labels_x = classif_fine,
  labels_y = classif_broad,
  relation = "is_contained_in",
  format = "matrix"
)
#>        y
#> x       0-19 20-59 60+
#>   0-9      1     0   0
#>   10-19    1     0   0
#>   20-29    0     1   0
#>   30-39    0     1   0
#>   40-49    0     1   0
#>   50-59    0     1   0
#>   60+      0     0   1

See Also

  • Adopt coarser age groups from another age variable
  • Aggregate to broader age groups
  • age_coarsen_to(), period_mapping(), cohort_mapping()

Use age, period, or cohort on the x-axis of a plot

Problem

You want to construct a plot with age, period, or cohort on the x-axis. But plots that use non-numeric age, period, or cohort labels on the x-axis often look terrible, and get categories in the wrong order.

df <- tibble(
  age = age_labels_five(),
  rate = 10 + 0.1 * (1:21)^2 + rnorm(21)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = age, y = rate)) +
  geom_point()

Solution

Convert age, period, or cohort to a continuous variable by using age_mid(), period_mid(), or cohort_mid().

ggplot(df, aes(x = age_mid(age), y = rate)) +
  geom_line()

See Also

  • Create an age variable that sorts properly
  • period_mid(), cohort_mid()

Calculate annual rates

Problem

Your data use multi-year periods, and you want annual rates.

Solution

Use period_width().

df <- tibble(
  period = c("2010-2020", "2020-2023", "2023-2030"),
  departures = c(2000, 50, 3000)
)

df |>
  mutate(
    n_year = period_width(period),
    annual_rate = departures / n_year
  )
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   period    departures n_year annual_rate
#>   <chr>          <dbl>  <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 2010-2020       2000     10       200  
#> 2 2020-2023         50      3        16.7
#> 3 2023-2030       3000      7       429.

Discussion

The width of an open interval is Inf.

See Also

  • age_width(), cohort_width()
